title: 1NF
description: Learn first normal form through meaningful domains, repeating memberships, row identity and lossless relationship modeling, with concrete campus design exercises.
notes:
## Represent one value from a declared domain

First normal form is the starting point for relational normalization. A relation should represent each attribute value as a value from its declared domain, without a repeating group of the same attribute inside a row. In practical SQL design, this often means moving a variable-length collection of related facts into a separate relation rather than storing a comma-separated list in one column or adding a fixed series of nearly identical columns.

The phrase atomic value is relative to the intended domain and operations. A date contains a year, month and day, yet it can be one value of the DATE domain. A text title contains words, yet it can be one title. The useful question is whether the design treats a cell as one domain value or hides several independently meaningful facts that the application must query and constrain separately.

## Identify the repeated fact in a campus example

Imagine learners with learner_id, learner_name and a column containing several skill codes such as SQL, PYTHON, LINUX. If each skill is independently searchable, assignable and removable, the cell hides multiple learner-skill relationships. An update that removes one skill must parse and reconstruct text instead of changing the one relationship that actually changed.

A better model has Learners(learner_id, learner_name) and LearnerSkills(learner_id, skill_code). The second relation holds one row for each learner-skill membership. A learner with three skills has three related rows. A learner with no recorded skills has no membership rows, while the learner entity still exists. This representation preserves the distinction between an entity and a collection of relationships about it.

## Replace repeating columns with rows

Columns named skill1, skill2 and skill3 expose the same problem in another form. The number of skills becomes a schema limit. Adding a fourth skill requires a new column or an awkward overflow convention. Searching all skills requires checking every slot, and the order of slots can accidentally acquire meaning even if membership is intended to be unordered.

Moving those values into rows removes the arbitrary slot count. Add a position or proficiency attribute only if the domain genuinely needs ordering or a measure for each membership. Do not preserve skill1 as a permanent concept merely because the old spreadsheet used that heading. Model the underlying fact first, then decide which attributes belong to that fact.

## Keep identity and multiplicity explicit

If the domain permits at most one membership per learner and skill, the pair can be a candidate key of LearnerSkills. If a learner can earn the same certification repeatedly in different years, learner plus skill no longer identifies the event. A certification attempt or award identity may be needed. The intended row meaning determines the key; a mechanical split of text does not choose it for you.

A surrogate identifier can identify a stored row without preventing duplicate memberships. If duplicate memberships are forbidden, a suitable uniqueness rule on the business pair is a separate invariant. Similarly, a foreign key can connect the membership to an existing learner. These constraints express integrity beyond merely presenting one skill code per cell, and actual application schema changes require their own approval and testing.

## Distinguish one string from a hidden collection

A learner biography is one textual document when the application stores and displays it as a document. The presence of commas does not make it a repeating group. A skill-code list is different when the application needs independent skill membership, exact matching, uniqueness and per-skill attributes. Delimiters are a symptom to investigate, not a formal rule that every comma violates normalization.

A location may be one address label for mailing, or it may need separately constrained country and postal fields for search and validation. That choice follows the operations and domain semantics. Avoid the extreme instruction to split every string into individual characters or every date into three columns. Decomposition should expose meaningful facts, not destroy useful scalar domains merely because their values have internal structure.

## Understand SQL support without confusing the model

SQL systems can support arrays, JSON values and other structured types. Their availability does not settle a relational modeling decision. A JSON document can be an appropriate stored document, but embedding independently managed learner-skill memberships in it changes how keys, references and updates are enforced. A design should describe that tradeoff honestly rather than claiming that every supported SQL type automatically satisfies every relational-normalization goal.

This lesson uses a conventional relational interpretation for independently queried memberships. It does not prohibit every JSON column or claim that all applications must decompose every document. What matters is whether the chosen representation supports the required integrity, access patterns and update ownership. [Normalization](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/functional-dependency) provides further dependency reasoning once the basic facts have a suitable relational shape.

## Preserve information while decomposing

When moving a learner's skills into rows, carry the learner identity into every membership. Splitting names and skills into unrelated tables loses which learner owns which skill. A later cross join would then manufacture memberships that never existed. The relationship key is not a technical decoration; it preserves the fact that the old row was trying to express.

Also distinguish an empty list, an unknown skill inventory and an invalid imported string if the domain cares about those states. Zero membership rows may mean no recorded memberships, but that alone cannot represent every possible workflow status. A separate verification status can express that a learner has not yet supplied information. Do not encode all those meanings by inventing a fake skill code such as UNKNOWN unless that code is genuinely part of the domain.

## Query the decomposed representation directly

Once the relationship is explicit, an exact membership lookup no longer needs substring search. A learner with skill code SQL is found by comparing the skill_code value, not by searching for those letters anywhere in a list. A substring search could incorrectly match a different code containing SQL or fail because of inconsistent separators and whitespace.

```sql
SELECT l.learner_id, l.learner_name
FROM learners AS l
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM learner_skills AS s
  WHERE s.learner_id = l.learner_id
    AND s.skill_code = 'SQL'
)
ORDER BY l.learner_id;
```

The query assumes a well-defined skill-code comparison contract. Case sensitivity and permitted code spelling should be decided by that domain. The schema shape makes the relationship addressable, but does not by itself decide whether sql and SQL are equivalent codes. Typed values, comparison rules and constraints remain necessary parts of a complete design.

## Recognize what first normal form does not guarantee

A relation containing learner_id, learner_name, course_id and course_title can have one value per cell while repeating learner and course descriptions on many enrollment rows. It may therefore satisfy the intended first-normal-form shape yet still have partial or transitive dependencies. First normal form is a foundation, not a claim that update anomalies have disappeared.

Likewise, choosing a primary key does not automatically resolve repeated facts hidden in other columns. A row_id beside a comma-separated skill list identifies the row but leaves the collection embedded. Keep the shape test separate from the key test and from later dependency tests. Continue with [2NF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/2nf) and [3NF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/3nf) to examine those additional responsibilities.

## Design from allowed facts

For a first design exercise, take a learner with three unordered skill memberships and another learner with none. Draw Learners and LearnerSkills, list their candidate keys, and show the five rows needed across the entity and membership relations to represent those facts. Explain why the second learner remains present even without a skill row. Then add a proficiency measure and decide which relation owns it.

For a second exercise, change the requirement to repeated certification awards over time. Explain why a learner-skill pair can no longer identify every award and propose the smallest additional identity information justified by that requirement. These are modeling exercises rather than query-output puzzles. They test whether the design preserves multiplicity, ownership and absence without inventing unsupported schema conventions.

## Define ordering only when it is a fact

A set of memberships does not inherently have first, second and third positions. If a learner ranks preferred skills, that rank is a real attribute of the learner-skill relationship and needs an explicit rule for ties or uniqueness. Reconstructing display text by sorting codes alphabetically is a presentation choice, not evidence that the original source encoded that order. During conversion, preserve order only when the domain says it matters, and avoid inventing a preference ranking from arbitrary spreadsheet slot placement. Conversely, if ordered steps are the actual fact, dropping their position loses information even when every resulting cell is scalar. First-normal-form reasoning should expose that position as data rather than treating all collections as interchangeable unordered lists.

## Review the representation before calling it normalized

A useful review asks what one row means, which attributes describe that fact, whether a cell hides independently managed memberships, and which constraints prevent invalid repetitions. Trace a representative insert, removal and lookup. If removing one skill requires editing an unrelated learner biography or shifting skill slots, the representation probably still mixes separate responsibilities.

The lesson's SQL illustrates one benefit of explicit relationships but does not prove a migration is safe. Converting existing collections requires parsing policy, invalid-value handling, deduplication rules and preservation checks before any actual schema work. The educational conclusion is narrower: represent the domain's independent facts so that their identities and relationships can be stated and enforced directly.

questions.question_text: Why does storing 'C1:Database Systems, C2:Operating Systems' in a single Courses cell violate 1NF?
options: Because the cell contains a colon character
Because the cell holds multiple values (a repeating group) instead of one atomic value per attribute
Because CourseName should never appear alongside CourseID
Because the cell is too long
questions.explanation: 1NF requires each cell to hold exactly one atomic value; packing multiple course memberships into one delimited string is a repeating group, the classic 1NF violation.

questions.question_text: How should independent unordered learner-skill memberships be represented in this model?
options: One learner biography containing every code
One LearnerSkills row per learner_id,skill_code membership
A new skill column for each learner
One global skill list without ownership
questions.explanation: Separate entity rows from membership rows and preserve the learner identity in each relationship.

questions.question_text: Can a table with one scalar domain value per cell still have partial or transitive dependency problems?
options: No, all dependencies disappear
Yes, first-normal-form shape alone does not establish 2NF or 3NF
Only if no primary key exists
Only if strings contain commas
questions.explanation: The shape test and higher dependency tests are separate. No historical course table is assumed.

questions.question_text: Why is skill1,skill2,skill3 a poor representation for an unbounded collection of independent memberships?
options: Every numbered attribute is forbidden regardless of meaning
It encodes repeating facts in fixed slots and makes collection growth require schema changes
Three columns always violate every normal form
The database cannot store a fourth row
questions.explanation: The problem is the repeated membership fact and arbitrary slot limit, not merely a number in a column name.

questions.question_text: For independently managed skill, phone and hobby memberships in this conventional relational model, which design is NOT a 1NF problem?
options: A single cell holding 'Python, Java, SQL' for a Skills attribute
A StudentName column split into separate FirstName and LastName columns
A single cell holding a JSON array of multiple phone numbers
Three columns Hobby1, Hobby2, Hobby3 used to store a variable number of hobbies
questions.explanation: Splitting a name into FirstName/LastName is a granularity design choice, not a 1NF issue — each of those columns still holds one atomic value. The other three options all encode multiple values of one conceptual attribute.

questions.question_text: Why does an ordinary foreign key on a delimited skill-list column not validate each embedded skill separately?
options: Foreign keys cannot reference strings
It compares the whole column value, not every parsed list element
Every comma is automatically a foreign key
Foreign keys validate every substring automatically
questions.explanation: Independent membership values allow ordinary relational references to validate the intended individual codes.

questions.question_text: What is the core requirement of First Normal Form?
options: Every non-key attribute must depend on the whole key
Every attribute value in every row must be atomic (single-valued), with no repeating groups
Every determinant must be a candidate key
There must be no transitive dependencies
questions.explanation: 1NF's sole concern is atomicity of values — the whole-key and transitive-dependency conditions belong to 2NF and 3NF respectively, which are separate, additional requirements.

questions.question_text: After converting the BEFORE table (one row per student, comma-separated courses) into the AFTER table (one row per student-course pair), what new capability is gained?
options: The ability to store more students
The ability to run a simple, indexable query like WHERE CourseID = 'C1' to find all students in that course, and to enforce a real foreign key into a Course table
Automatic removal of all update anomalies
The elimination of the need for a primary key
questions.explanation: Achieving 1NF makes each course membership an atomic, queryable, indexable, and foreign-key-able value — but it does NOT by itself remove the update/insertion/deletion anomalies, which need 2NF/3NF.

questions.question_text: What is the strongest reason to separate learner skills into rows?
options: Each membership is independently queried and constrained
Every comma is forbidden in SQL
Strings can never be domain values
A date must be split into characters
questions.explanation: The independent fact determines the relational shape.

questions.question_text: Does a comma in a biography necessarily violate 1NF?
options: Yes always
No
Only when an index exists
Only in MySQL
questions.explanation: One document value differs from a hidden collection of relationships.

questions.question_text: A learner adds a fourth independently managed skill after the old design reached skill1,skill2,skill3. What does the relationship-row design allow?
options: Drop an earlier skill to reuse its slot
Add a fourth permanent column for every learner
Add one membership row without changing the schema
Store the extra skill in the learner name
questions.explanation: A row-per-membership design lets collection size grow as facts, while fixed slots tie capacity to the schema.

questions.question_text: What does a learner with no memberships require?
options: Deleting the learner
A fake SQL skill
One NULL skill row for every possible code
A learner row and no membership rows
questions.explanation: Entity existence is separate from membership existence.

questions.question_text: When is learner_id,skill_code a suitable candidate key?
options: When at most one such membership is allowed
Whenever the columns are printed first
Even when repeated awards are separate events
Only if skill codes are numeric
questions.explanation: Key choice follows permitted multiplicity.

questions.question_text: What can a surrogate row ID fail to prevent?
options: Identification of a stored row
Duplicate business memberships
Every possible query
All foreign keys
questions.explanation: A row identifier is not automatically business-pair uniqueness.

questions.question_text: Why carry learner_id into membership rows?
options: To sort skill names automatically
To replace every other key
To preserve ownership of each relationship
To prohibit empty memberships
questions.explanation: Without the relationship key reconstruction loses the original associations.

questions.question_text: Does 1NF eliminate every update anomaly?
options: Yes, every dependency is resolved
Only when SELECT * is used
Only with integer IDs
No
questions.explanation: Higher normal forms examine additional dependencies.

questions.question_text: Why avoid substring search for an exact skill membership?
options: It can match fragments of another code
SQL cannot compare strings
EXISTS always changes storage
Substring search is always a syntax error
questions.explanation: Explicit values support the intended exact comparison.

questions.question_text: What extra requirement changes a membership pair into an insufficient award key?
options: A longer learner name
Repeated awards of the same skill over time
An ORDER BY clause
A renamed table alias
questions.explanation: Multiple event facts can share the membership pair.

questions.question_text: Does SQL support for JSON settle the normalization choice?
options: Yes, JSON always means full normalization
Yes, JSON is never usable
No, domain and integrity requirements still matter
Only when JSON text contains no commas
questions.explanation: Structured storage capability is distinct from fact modeling.

questions.question_text: What should an actual collection migration define first?
options: Only the new table name
Only the number of columns
Only the output color
Parsing, invalid-value, deduplication and preservation policies
questions.explanation: Changing representation can otherwise lose or invent facts.

coding_not_applicable: This topic assesses relational representation and preservation of membership facts. The notes contain two explicit schema-design exercises, including zero memberships and repeated awards. SQL output against an already chosen schema would not validate the modeling decision; a read-only membership example illustrates the consequence without claiming an executable proof of 1NF.

original_questions.question_text: What is the correct 1NF transformation of the BEFORE table with the comma-separated Courses column?
options: Delete the Courses column entirely
Split each student's course list into separate rows, one per (StudentID, CourseID) pairing, as done in the StudentCourse table used throughout this chapter
Store the list as a single JSON array in the same cell
Add more columns like Course1, Course2, Course3
original_questions.explanation: 1NF is achieved by giving each (student, course) fact its own atomic row rather than packing multiple courses into one cell — exactly how StudentCourse is structured.

original_questions.question_text: Has the StudentCourse table used throughout topics 21.1-21.11 ever violated 1NF?
options: Yes, because it has a composite key
No — every attribute in every row has always held a single atomic value; its redundancy and anomaly problems come from partial/transitive dependency issues (2NF/3NF), not atomicity
Yes, because InstructorOffice repeats across rows
No, but only after topic 21.13's decomposition
original_questions.explanation: 1NF is only about atomicity of values, which StudentCourse always satisfied. Its problems were caused by violations of 2NF and 3NF, which are separate, stricter conditions.

original_questions.question_text: Why is a fixed set of columns like Course1, Course2, Course3 (instead of a comma-separated string) still considered a 1NF violation?
options: Because it isn't a violation at all — fixed columns always satisfy 1NF
Because it still encodes a variable-length, multi-valued fact using a rigid structure, and can't handle a student with more courses than there are columns, nor be queried/indexed the relational way
Because column names cannot include numbers
Because it uses more storage than a comma-separated string
original_questions.explanation: Spreading a repeating group across multiple fixed columns is just a different disguise for the same underlying multi-valued-attribute problem that 1NF forbids.

original_questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a 1NF violation?
options: A single cell holding 'Python, Java, SQL' for a Skills attribute
A StudentName column split into separate FirstName and LastName columns
A single cell holding a JSON array of multiple phone numbers
Three columns Hobby1, Hobby2, Hobby3 used to store a variable number of hobbies

original_questions.question_text: Why can't a foreign key constraint be enforced on the CourseID values embedded inside a comma-separated Courses string?
options: Foreign keys can be enforced on any text pattern

A foreign key constraint requires a column value to reference a specific row in another table, which is impossible when the value is buried inside free-form delimited text rather than being its own atomic column value
Because CourseID must always be numeric for foreign keys to work
Because foreign keys are incompatible with 1NF
original_questions.explanation: Relational integrity constraints operate on discrete column values; text embedded inside a larger string isn't a distinct value the database engine can validate against another table.
